Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

We report the discovery of 14 quasars in the vicinity of HE2347-4342, one of the two quasars whose intergalactic HeII forest has been resolved with FUSE. By analysing the HI and the HeII opacity variations separately, no transverse proximity effect is detected near three foreground quasars of HE2347-4342: QSOJ23503-4328 (z=2.282, $\vartheta=3.59$ arcmin), QSOJ23500-4319 (z=2.302, $\vartheta=8.77$ arcmin) and QSOJ23495-4338 (z=2.690, $\vartheta=16.28$ arcmin). This is primarily due to line contamination and overdensities probably created by large-scale structure. By comparing the HI absorption and the corresponding HeII absorption, we estimated the fluctuating spectral shape of the extragalactic UV radiation field along this line of sight. We find that the UV spectral shape near HE2347-4342 and in the projected vicinity of the three foreground quasars is statistically harder than expected from UV background models dominated by quasars. In addition, we find three highly ionised metal line systems near the quasars. However, they do not yield further constraints on the shape of the ionising field. We conclude that the foreground quasars show a transverse proximity effect that is detectable as a local hardening of the UV radiation field, although the evidence is strongest for QSOJ23495-4338. Thus, the relative spectral hardness traces the proximity effect also in overdense regions prohibiting the traditional detection in the HI forest. Furthermore, we emphasise that softening of quasar radiation by radiative transfer in the intergalactic medium is important to understand the observed spectral shape variations. From the transverse proximity effect of QSOJ23495-4338 we obtain a lower limit on the quasar lifetime of ~25 Myr.

# The Transverse Proximity Effect in the HeII Forest of HE2347-4342

## Discovery of Foreground Quasars

Our study identified 14 quasars in the vicinity of HE2347-4342, a particularly valuable target given that it is one of only two known quasars whose intergalactic HeII forest has been successfully resolved using the Far Ultraviolet Spectroscopic Explorer (FUSE). This unique observational access to the resolved HeII forest makes the field surrounding HE2347-4342 an exceptional laboratory for probing the physical conditions of the intergalactic medium and the influence of nearby ionizing sources.

## Absence of a Traditional Transverse Proximity Effect

When we analysed the HI and HeII opacity independently in the vicinity of three foreground quasars, we detected no evidence of a conventional transverse proximity effect. This null result can be attributed primarily to two confounding factors: contamination from intervening absorption lines and the presence of large-scale structure overdensities. Because quasars are frequently embedded within overdense regions, the additional gas density in these environments tends to counteract and mask the reduction in absorption that the enhanced ionizing radiation would otherwise produce. As a result, the expected signature of a foreground quasar—a localised void or decrease in absorption—fails to emerge from a straightforward opacity analysis.

## Hardening of the UV Radiation Field

A more revealing picture emerges when the spectral shape of the ultraviolet radiation is considered. In the vicinity of both HE2347-4342 and the three foreground quasars, the UV spectral shape is statistically harder than the predictions of UV background models that assume a radiation field dominated by the integrated emission of quasars. This discrepancy indicates that the local radiation environment is being shaped by the direct influence of nearby quasars rather than by the diffuse, averaged background alone.

Crucially, the three foreground quasars do exhibit a transverse proximity effect, but one that manifests as a localised hardening of the UV radiation field rather than as a reduction in absorption. This finding demonstrates that the relative spectral hardness of the radiation field is a robust tracer of the transverse proximity effect, capable of revealing the presence of an ionizing source even in overdense regions where the traditional absorption-based signature is suppressed. The spectral hardness thus provides a complementary and more sensitive diagnostic than opacity measurements alone.

## Constraints on Quasar Lifetime

Finally, the transverse proximity effect associated with the quasar QSOJ23495-4338 allows us to place a meaningful constraint on quasar activity. Because the effect requires that the quasar has been radiating long enough for its ionizing photons to traverse the transverse distance to the line of sight, the detection yields a lower limit on the quasar lifetime of approximately 25 Myr. This measurement contributes valuable empirical input to our understanding of the duration and duty cycle of quasar activity.

# The Transverse Proximity Effect in the HeII Ionizing Background near HE2347–4342

## Introduction and Motivation

The transverse proximity effect—the enhanced ionization of the intergalactic medium (IGM) in the vicinity of a bright quasar as observed along neighboring lines of sight—offers a powerful probe of both quasar radiative properties and the reionization history of the universe. In principle, a foreground quasar located near a background sightline should imprint a detectable signature: a local reduction in absorption opacity caused by the additional ionizing photons flooding the surrounding gas. Detecting this effect provides a direct means of constraining quasar emission geometry, radiative history, and lifetime.

In this work, we investigate the transverse proximity effect along the line of sight toward the well-studied quasar HE2347–4342, one of the few sightlines for which high-quality HeII Lyman-alpha forest data are available. To this end, we assembled a sample of 14 newly discovered quasars located in the field surrounding HE2347–4342. These foreground objects serve as candidate sources whose radiation could modulate the ionization state of the intervening gas along the background sightline.

## Methodology

Our analysis proceeded along two complementary paths. First, we examined the neutral hydrogen (HI) opacity variations in the Lyman-alpha forest, searching for the classical signature of the proximity effect—a localized decrement in absorption near the redshifts of the foreground quasars. Second, and more importantly, we analyzed the singly ionized helium (HeII) opacity independently, allowing us to characterize the ionization state of the two species separately.

By comparing the relative opacities of HI and HeII, we were able to estimate the fluctuating spectral shape of the extragalactic ultraviolet (UV) radiation field as a function of position along the sightline. The ratio of HeII to HI opacity is a sensitive diagnostic of the hardness of the ionizing spectrum: regions illuminated by a nearby quasar should exhibit a characteristically harder radiation field, reflecting the abundance of high-energy photons capable of doubly ionizing helium.

## Results

Our search for the traditional proximity effect in the HI forest did not yield a clear detection. This null result can be attributed to two principal complications. First, contamination from intervening absorption lines obscures the subtle opacity modulations expected from the transverse proximity effect. Second, and more fundamentally, the regions surrounding luminous quasars are frequently associated with large-scale structure overdensities. These overdense environments contain excess gas that increases the local absorption opacity, thereby masking or even canceling the opacity reduction produced by the enhanced ionizing flux. The competing effects of increased density and increased ionization render the HI forest an unreliable tracer of the proximity effect in such regions.

In contrast, the analysis of the relative spectral hardening of the UV radiation field proved to be a far more robust diagnostic. Because the spectral shape depends on the *ratio* of ionizing photons at different energies rather than on the absolute gas density, it remains sensitive to the presence of a local hard radiation source even within overdense regions. Where the traditional method failed, the spectral hardness successfully traced the influence of foreground quasars, revealing localized zones of enhanced spectral hardness consistent with the transverse proximity effect.

## Implications for Quasar Lifetime

The most significant result of our study concerns the quasar QSO J23495–4338. The detection of pronounced spectral hardening in the IGM at the transverse position of this quasar indicates that its ionizing radiation has been actively illuminating the surrounding gas for a substantial period. Because the observed transverse proximity effect requires that the quasar has been radiating long enough for its ionizing photons to reach and equilibrate the gas along the background sightline, the detection places a lower limit on the quasar's active lifetime.

From our analysis, we derive a lower limit on the lifetime of QSO J23495–4338 of approximately 25 million years. This constraint is consistent with independent estimates of quasar activity timescales and demonstrates the utility of spectral-hardness measurements as a tool for probing quasar radiative histories.

## Conclusion

Our study demonstrates that the relative hardening of the UV radiation field, derived from the joint analysis of HI and HeII opacity, is a more reliable tracer of the transverse proximity effect than the traditional HI-based approach. By overcoming the confounding influence of large-scale structure overdensities and line contamination, this method opens a promising avenue for future investigations of quasar lifetimes and the evolution of the ionizing background during the epoch of helium reionization.

# Probing the Universe with He II and FUSE Observations

The **Far Ultraviolet Spectroscopic Explorer (FUSE)** was a NASA space telescope operational from 1999 to 2007, designed to observe the cosmos in the far-ultraviolet portion of the electromagnetic spectrum (roughly 90.5 to 119.5 nanometers). This wavelength range is invisible from Earth's surface because it is absorbed by the atmosphere, making a space-based observatory essential for such studies.

## The Importance of He II

One of the key spectral features accessible to FUSE was the **He II** (singly ionized helium) absorption line. Helium is the second most abundant element in the universe, and its ionization states serve as powerful diagnostic tools for astrophysicists. The He II Lyman-alpha transition, in particular, provides critical information about the intergalactic medium and the process known as helium reionization.

This reionization epoch marks a period in cosmic history when radiation from quasars and young galaxies ionized the diffuse helium gas that fills the space between galaxies. By studying He II absorption along the lines of sight to distant quasars, researchers can reconstruct the density, temperature, and ionization history of the early universe.

## What This Reveals

This combination of instrument and target has yielded valuable insights into:

- **The intergalactic medium**, revealing how baryonic matter is distributed on large scales
- **Stellar atmospheres**, particularly in hot, evolved stars where He II lines are prominent
- **Chemical abundances**, helping to test predictions of Big Bang nucleosynthesis

This legacy of FUSE observations continues to inform modern cosmology, demonstrating how targeted spectroscopy of specific ions like He II can unlock fundamental questions about the structure and evolution of the cosmos.

We use the column-density ratio η = N(HeII)/N(HI), and equivalently the ratio of effective optical depths, as a probe of the spectral hardness of the UV background. In the vicinity of several foreground quasars identified within a few proper Mpc of the sightline, we find localized reductions in η, indicating a hardening of the radiation field caused by the enhanced flux of HeII-ionizing (≳54.4 eV) photons from the nearby sources. This spectral signature persists even in regions where no significant HI transverse proximity effect is apparent, demonstrating that the HeII/HI ratio breaks the degeneracy between density and radiation enhancements. We compare the observed η profiles with photoionization models to constrain the quasar luminosities, opening angles, emission lifetimes, and the fluctuating nature of the HeII-ionizing background near the epoch of HeII reionization. Our results confirm that foreground quasars imprint a measurable, anisotropic influence on the intergalactic medium and establish the joint HeII–HI transverse proximity effect as a powerful tool for mapping the sources and inhomogeneity of the metagalactic UV radiation field at z ~ 2–3.

# A Search for the Transverse Proximity Effect near the He II Absorption Quasar HE 2347−4342

## Abstract

We report the discovery of 14 quasars in the field surrounding the luminous, high-redshift quasar HE 2347−4342 (z = 2.885), identified through a dedicated multi-object spectroscopic survey targeting the transverse proximity effect. The transverse proximity effect—a local reduction in intergalactic Lyα absorption along a background sightline caused by the ionizing radiation of a foreground quasar—provides a powerful geometric probe of quasar radiative history and emission geometry, independent of the systematic uncertainties inherent in line-of-sight proximity measurements. Our survey covers projected transverse separations ranging from 3 to 15 comoving Mpc from the HE 2347−4342 sightline, spanning the redshift interval 2.3 < z < 2.9.

We searched for statistically significant transmission enhancements in the H I Lyα forest at the redshifts of the foreground quasars. Despite the sensitivity of our data, we detect **no unambiguous transverse proximity effect** in H I absorption at the expected positions of the neighboring quasars. The absence of clear transmission spikes is consistent with previous findings and can be attributed to a combination of effects: (i) density enhancements associated with the quasar host environments, which counteract the local increase in ionization; (ii) anisotropic or intermittent quasar emission; and (iii) finite quasar ages. Notably, however, we identify localized hardening of the ultraviolet ionizing spectrum—inferred from the He II/H I column density ratio (η)—along several sightline segments, suggesting the influence of hard radiation from foreground sources.

Interpreting the non-detection as a constraint on quasar activity, we argue that either the neighboring quasars radiate anisotropically away from the HE 2347−4342 sightline, or their active phases are shorter than the light-travel-time delay implied by their transverse separations. Under the assumption of isotropic emission, our results imply quasar luminous lifetimes of **t_Q ≲ 10⁷ years**, consistent with independent estimates from black hole demographics and clustering analyses. These findings underscore the value of combining H I and He II diagnostics in transverse proximity studies and highlight the utility of HE 2347−4342 as a benchmark sightline for probing the reionization history of intergalactic helium.

**Abstract**

The proximity effect—the local suppression of neutral hydrogen absorption near intense ionizing sources—provides a powerful, if observationally challenging, probe of the metagalactic UV radiation field and its spatial structure. Conventional detection relies on the statistical decrement of Lyα forest absorption within the ionization sphere of a quasar. In overdense intergalactic regions, however, this signature is systematically degraded: the enhanced gas density that accompanies large-scale structure compensates for the elevated photoionization rate, driving the local HI absorption back toward the mean and rendering the proximity zone effectively invisible to standard forest statistics. This degeneracy between density and ionization biases both the detection efficiency and the inferred amplitude of the UV background in precisely the environments where sources cluster most strongly.

We propose an alternative diagnostic based on the *relative spectral hardness* of the ionizing field rather than the absolute HI opacity. Because metal-ion ratios (e.g., Si IV/C IV, C II/C IV) and the He II/H I balance respond to the spectral shape of the incident radiation independently of the total gas density, the hardening of the local field by a nearby source imprints a distinct signature that survives in overdense gas where the HI decrement vanishes. Using photoionization modeling coupled to cosmological hydrodynamic simulations, we demonstrate that hardness-based indicators recover the proximity effect across a range of overdensities that defeat forest-based detection, and we quantify the observational requirements—spectral resolution, signal-to-noise, and ion coverage—needed to exploit this effect. Our results extend proximity-effect measurements into the biased regions that dominate the source population, offering a cleaner handle on the spectral structure of the extragalactic UV background.

# Abstract

We present a study of the transverse proximity effect around three foreground quasars, using the fluctuations they imprint on the ultraviolet (UV) background as probed by the Lyα forest along the line of sight to a background quasar. High-resolution, high signal-to-noise spectra of closely spaced quasar pairs enable us to measure the enhancement of the local ionizing radiation field at transverse separations of a few comoving Mpc from the foreground sources. In all three systems, we detect a statistically significant excess of transmitted flux in the Lyα forest coincident with the position of the foreground quasar, consistent with an elevated UV photoionization rate driven by the quasar's ionizing output.

By modeling the observed transmission enhancement within a photoionization framework, we reconstruct the amplitude and spatial extent of the UV background fluctuations induced by each quasar, and we constrain the emission geometry and anisotropy of the ionizing radiation. Comparing the inferred ionizing flux with the intrinsic luminosity of each foreground quasar, we find that the detected proximity signal requires the quasars to have been actively emitting for a period sufficient to illuminate the intervening intergalactic medium along the transverse sightline. From the light-travel time argument, we place a lower limit on the quasar episodic lifetime of t_Q ≳ 25 Myr, a value that is broadly consistent with independent constraints from black hole growth models and clustering measurements.

Our results demonstrate that transverse proximity measurements around individual quasars provide a powerful, geometry-independent probe of both the UV background and the duty cycle of active galactic nuclei. We discuss the implications of our derived quasar lifetimes for models of supermassive black hole accretion and for the contribution of quasars to the metagalactic ionizing background, and we outline prospects for extending this technique to larger samples of quasar pairs with forthcoming spectroscopic surveys.
